div.p: In this paper, we are interested in the energyefficient scheduling of real-time tasks on a non-ideal DVS processor. We assume that tasks are periodic, preemptive, dynamic priority, and may concurrent access to a set of shared resources. Based on the well-known earliest deadline first (EDF) algorithm and the stack resource policy (SRP), we propose an approach, called blocking-aware two-speed (BATS) algorithm, to calculate appropriate speeds for task execution. In particular, tasks are executed at a static low speed when blocking does not occur, and a high speed will be calculated dynamically whenever a task blocks a higher priority task. The processor must run at the high speed from the beginning of the blocking until the deadline of the blocked task or the processor becomes idle. The low speed and the high speed are derived based on the theoretical analysis of the schedulability of tasks so that the energy consumption can be reduced without violating the timing constraints of tasks. Compare with existing work, BATS achieves more energy saving because its derived high speeds are lower than that of existing work and the processor has less time to execute tasks at the high speeds.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: When dynamic voltage scaling (DVS) is employed, tasks can be executed at a lower processor speed and the overall energy consumption can be reduced. However, the slowdown of the processor speed will cause an impact on performance due to the late completion of tasks. It provides a strong driving force in energy-efficient scheduling of real-time tasks due to the fact that the late completion is allowed as long as the tasks meet their timing requirements (i.e., deadlines). Many excellent approaches have been proposed for scheduling of real-time tasks on a DVS processor. Chen and Kuo [1] have presented a comprehensive survey of the energy-efficient real-time scheduling. Most previous studies assume that tasks are independent, relatively little work has been done in the presence of task synchronization.

For real-time tasks with shared resources, existing approaches mainly focus on tasks with non-preemptible critical sections [2], [3], [4], [5], [6]. Zhang and Chanson [2], [3] first proposed a two-speed strategy (TSS), called dual speed (DS) algorithm. When tasks are scheduled by the well-known earliest deadline first (EDF) [7] algorithm, DS calculates the low speed and the high speed based on the sufficient schedulability condition of EDF. Hence, the timing constraints of tasks can be met while energy consumption is reduced. In particular, DS assigns the low speed for executing tasks when they arrive, and the processor speed switches to the high speed as soon as the tasks are blocked. Later, some TSS-based approaches (e.g., [4], [5], [6]) have extended from this direction. In particular, Lee et al. [4] explored the same problem with a tighter schedulability analysis, and proposed a multi-speed extension of DS, called multi-speed (MS) algorithm. MS assigns different high speeds for each task by considering different blocking scenarios of task instances. MS reduces more energy consumption than that of DS, and the schedulability of the tasks is still guaranteed.

Making critical sections non-preemptible is not desirable because the blocking time and the number of priority inversions might be increased, and it might result in a higher processor speed than it required for task synchronization. When critical sections are considered to be preemptible, Jejurikar and Gupta have proposed some TSS-based scheduling algorithms (e.g., [8], [9]). In particular, they proposed uniform slowdown with frequency inheritance (USFI) algorithm [9] to compute a static speed for each task based on the schedulability analysis of tasks with their worst-case blocking time. To achieve more energy saving, researchers also proposed TSS-based algorithms with the slack time stealing method, such as [10]. Recently, Wu and Kao [11] also proposed a more energyefficient TSS-based approach by assuming that critical sections are abortable.

In this paper, we are interested in scheduling and synchronizing of preemptible tasks (both of critical sections and non-critical sections). A TSS-based approach, called blockingaware two-speed (BATS) algorithm, is proposed to schedule a set of real-time tasks with shared resources on a non-ideal DVS processor. Our proposed BATS can be viewed as an extension of MS [4]. However, different from MS, BATS is proposed for tasks with preemptible critical sections and can function with real-time concurrency control protocol to ensure the data consistency of shared resources. We use the wellknown earliest deadline first (EDF) algorithm [7] and the stack resource policy (SRP) [12] for scheduling and synchronizing of tasks, respectively. Our proposed BATS calculates a static low and dynamic high speeds for task executions. Under BATS, a task will be executed at the low speed if blocking does not happen, and the processor speed will with to a high speed which is calculated dynamically whenever a blocking occurs.

The processor operates at the high speed from the beginning of the blocking until the deadline of the blocked task or the processor becomes idle. Under BATS, the low speed and the high speed are derived based on the theoretical analysis of the schedulability of tasks. As the result, the energy consumption can be reduced without violating the timing constraints of tasks.

The major contributions of this research are two-fold: (1) We explore the DVS scheduling problem under a more realistic task model. Particularly, we consider tasks are dependent due to concurrent access to shared resources. (2) We explore the schedulability of tasks when they are scheduled by BATS on a non-ideal DVS processor. Related issues of how to derive proper processor speeds and when to change the processor speed between the low and the high speeds are also discussed. Furthermore, the dynamically derived high speeds of BATS are lower than that of the existing work, and the processor has less time to execute tasks at the high speed. As a result, BATS achieves more energy saving.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II defines the system model and the problem. Section III proposes BATS with properties and schedulability analysis. Section IV reports the performance evaluation. Section V is the conclusion.

div.head: II. SYSTEM MODEL AND PROBLEM DEFINITIONS A. DVS Processor Models
div.p: In this paper, the assumptions on the processor model and the power consumption function are widely adopted in the literatures (e.g., [13], [14], [9], [15], [2], [5], [6]). We assume that a set of real-time tasks are scheduled on a non-ideal DVS processor which supports a set of k discrete speeds
div.formula: S = {s 1 , s 2 , • • • , s k }, where s 1 < s 2 < • • • < s k .
div.p: Note that the processor speed is approximately proportional to the supply voltage. The supply voltage of a processor speed s i is denoted by V i , for 1 ≤ i ≤ k. Let s min and s max denote the minimum and the maximum speeds (i.e., s min = s 1 and s max = s k ), respectively. Without lose of generality, we assume the s max is 1 and all other speeds are normalized with respect to the maximum speed s max .

The power consumption function P C(s) of processor speed s can be divided into two parts: dynamic and static power. The dynamic power consumption P C dynamic (s), due to gate switching at processor speed s, can be modeled as a convex function of the processor speed:

Since the supply voltage V dd is the dominant source of the dynamic and the static power consumption. div.head: B. Task and Resource Models
div.p: We consider a hard real-time system that consists of a set of n tasks T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n }. Tasks are assumed to be periodic, preemptible, fixed-priority, and dependent due to concurrent accesses to shared resources. A task τ i is defined by a tuple
div.formula: (P i , A i , T i , D i , C i , Z i ), where P i , A i , T i , D i , C i ,
div.p: and Z i are the task's priority, arrival time, period, relative deadline, worst-case computation amount, and a list of critical sections, respectively. We assume that tasks are well formed which satisfy the condition:
div.formula: 0 ≤ C i ≤ D i ≤ T i , ∀τ i ∈ τ .
div.p: A task is a template of its instance and each instance will be instantiated for every request of the task. In particular, the first request of τ i arrives at time A i and the reminder requests will arrive regularly for every period T i . Let τ i,j and A i,j denote the jth instance of task τ i and its arrival time (i.e., instantiate time), respectively. The worst-case execution time of each task instance τ i,j is no more than C i /s j when it is executed at speed s j1 . We say a task instance τ i,j meets the deadline if it is completed at or before its deadline (i.e., A i,j + D i ), and it misses the deadline otherwise.

In this paper, we are interested in scheduling and synchronizing of real-time tasks with shared resources. We assume a set of m shared resources (e.g., shared variables, data objects, or files) R = {r 1 , r 2 , . . . , r m } can be accessed in the system. Shared resources do not allow to be accessed simultaneously. We assume that the access control of shared resources is guarded by semaphores to guarantee a mutual exclusion among competing tasks. A piece of code that accesses a shared resource under mutual exclusion constraints is called a critical section. The critical sections of a task τ i is defined by a list Z i =< z i,1 , z i,2 , . . . , z i,ni >, where z i,j is the jth critical section of τ i . To maintain data consistency, a task must lock the corresponding semaphore before it enters a critical section and unlock the semaphore after the access of the critical section has been completed. A task instance τ i,j is said to be blocked when its lock request is rejected due to the conflict access with another lower priority task. The worst-case blocking time of a task τ i is denoted by B i which is the maximal blocking time of all task instances of τ i . We also assume that critical sections are properly nested. In particular, locks are released in the reverse order from which they were obtained.

div.head: C. Problem Definitions
div.p: Let lcm denotes the least common multiple of all tasks' periods (also called hyperperiod). Since the task set T repeats an identical execution trace every hyperperiod, we only need to examine the time interval (0, lcm] for analyzing the performance and schedulability of the entire schedule [7]. The research problem is as follows:

Problem 1: Energy-Efficient Scheduling and Synchronization of Real-Time Tasks with Shared Resources Given a set of n real-time tasks T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , . . . , τ n } and a set of m shared resources R = {r 1 , r 2 , • • • , r m }. The problem is to schedule T and to synchronize their accesses of R on a non-ideal DVS processor which supports a set of k discrete speeds S = {s min = s 1 , s 2 , • • • , s k = s max }. During a given time interval (0, lcm], the objective of this problem is to generate a schedule such that all tasks can meet their timing requirements (i.e., their deadlines) and the energy consumption
div.formula: lcm 0 P C(s(t)) dt is minimized.

div.head: A. Task Scheduling and Concurrency Control
div.p: Our proposed BATS uses EDF [7] and SRP as its scheduling policy and concurrency control mechanism. It always schedule tasks with sooner deadlines first, followed by longer periods if tasks have the same deadlines. A fixed value, called preemption level, is assigned to each task for predicting the potential blocking in the presence of dynamic-priority scheduling [12]. Let π i be the preemption level of a task τ i . The essential property of preemption levels is that a task τ i can preempt another task τ j only if π i > π j . Under BATS algorithm, the preemption levels of tasks are assigned inversely proportional to its relative deadline (i.e., π i > π j ⇔ D i < D j ).

Each resource r j has a ceiling CL rj which is the highest preemption level of all the tasks that require the resource r j . We also define the system ceiling CL s which is the highest ceiling of all the resources that are in use currently. Note that the system ceiling CL s is 0 when all the resources are free, and it is updated each time a resource is allocated to a task or freed. A task τ i is not permitted to preempt the current task until its priority is the highest among those of the tasks ready to run, and its preemption level is higher than the system ceiling, i.e., π i > CL s .

Theorem 1: When a set of tasks is scheduled under BATS algorithm, then 1) no task can be blocked after it starts; 2) a task can be blocked for at most the duration of one critical section. Proof. The theorem follows directly from the theories of SRP [12].

According to Theorem 1, the maximum time which a low priority task τ j can block another high priority task is no more than the maximum length of a critical section of τ j . Note that the actual blocking time of a task τ i is no more than B j if τ i is blocked by a τ j 's critical section z j,k where B j is the remaining computation of z j,k . For example, B j = |z j,k |x if z j,k has been executed for x time units before τ j blocks τ i .

div.head: B. Execution Speed
div.p: The goal of this subsection is to derive the execution speeds of tasks so that the energy consumption can be reduced without violating their timing constraints. In order to reach this goal, we will derive two processor speeds, called the low speed and the high speed. The low speed, denoted as L, is assigned to a task instance if it will not be blocked by other lower-priority tasks; the high speed, denoted as H i , is assigned to a task instance of τ i if it might be blocked by other lower-priority tasks. In particular, BATS algorithm initially executes tasks at the low speed, denoted as L, then it switches to a high speed when a blocking occurs.

The derivation of the low sped L is based on the well-known schedulability analysis of EDF. Let T = {τ 1 , τ 2 , • • • , τ n } be the tasks ordered in non-decreasing order of their periods. Assuming that the tasks are independent (i.e., without access to shared resources), the following theorem derives a static (fixed) processor speed to reduce the energy consumption without violating the timing constraints of independent tasks.
Theorem 2: ([14], [13]) Given a set of n independent periodic tasks on EDF scheduling policy, they can be feasibly scheduled at a minimum processor speed L if
div.formula: L = min sx∈S {s x : n i=1 C i T i ≤ s x } (1)
div.p: Theorem 2 does not consider the effect of a task being blocked by lower-priority tasks. For dependent tasks (due to concurrent accesses to shared resources), the blocking time due to conflict access of shared resources must be considered. Hence, the low speed L can be viewed as a lower bound for tasks. We will assign L to every task instance when it will not be blocked by other lower-priority tasks.
We shall derive the high speed H i for each task τ i dynamically when it is blocked by a lower priority task τ j (tasks are ordered in non-decreasing order of their periods):
div.formula: H i = min sx∈S {s x : B j + i k=1 Ti T k C k T i ≤ s x } (2)
div.p: Where the B j is the actual blocking time through which τ j can block τ i . Under BATS, a task will be blocked when it becomes the highest priority task among all tasks ready to run and its preemption level is no larger than the system ceiling (i.e., π i ≤ CL s ). Whenever a task τ i is blocked by a low priority task τ j , BATS switches the processor speed to H i until the deadline of τ i or the time that the processor becomes idle.

div.head: C. The BATS algorithm
div.p: Algorithm 1 is our proposed BATS algorithm. Initially, all tasks are executed at the low speed L in Equation ( 1) and then switch to the high speed H i in Equation (2) whenever a task τ i is blocked. Note that the time complexity for calculating the low speed is O(n), where n is the number of tasks in the systems (it is known in a prior). The time intervals that the processor is running at a high speed are called high speed intervals. When a task τ i is blocked by a low priority task τ j , i.e., π i ≤ CL s , BATS algorithm will calculate H i dynamically and switch the processor speed to H i in order to meet all tasks' timing constraints. The time complexity for calculating the high speed of τ i is O(n), where n is the number of tasks with higher or equal priority of task τ i . Note that it need not switch the processor speed if the current processor speed is already greater than H i due to other previous blocking.

The processor keeps the high speed until the deadline of the blocked (high priority) task (i.e., τ i 's deadline) or the time that the processor becomes idle. We denote the time at the end of a high speed interval as End H. After the time reaches End H, the processor speed can be restored to L. If the processor is idle, its speed can be restored to L as well.

div.head: D. Example
div.p: We shall illustrate our proposed BATS with the following example.

Example 1: (A BATS Schedule) Consider three tasks, given in Figure 1, have to be executed on a DVS processor. The speeds of the DVS processor are from 0.05 to 1 increased by 0.05, i.e., s min = s 1 = 0.05, s 2 = 0.1, s 3 = 0.15, • • • , s 20 = s max = 1. According to the periods of the three tasks, the preemption level of τ 1 , τ 2 , and τ 3 are 3, 2, and 1, respectively (where 3 is the highest and 1 is the lowest). Note that their deadlines are assumed to be equal to their periods. We assume that a shared resource r x is accessed by all three tasks. The ceiling CL rx is 3 which is the highest preemption level of tasks that require r x . According to Equation (1), the low speed L is 0.5. Figure 2 shows the schedule of the three tasks under our proposed BATS from time 0 to 24 which is the least common multiple of tasks' periods.

At time 0, all three tasks are arrived, τ 1 starts its execution at the low speed L = 0.5 because it has a shortest deadline. At time 2, τ 1 is completed and τ 2 becomes the highest priority task. Hence, τ 2 starts its execution and lock r x successfully. At time 4, a new instance of τ 1 is arrived with a deadline shorter than the current task (i.e., τ 2 ). However, because the preemption level of τ 1 is not higher than the system ceiling CL s = 3, τ 1 is blocked by τ 2 . According to BATS, tasks should be executed at the high speed of τ 1 (i.e., H 1 ) until τ 1 's deadline or the time that processor is idle. Based on Equation ( 2) and B 2 = 0.5, the value of H 1 is 0.4. However, we still uses speed 0.5 for task execution because H 1 is less than the current processor speed. Note that this interval is marked as a high speed interval for ease of comparison. Later, τ 2 is completed at time 5, and then τ 1 is executed from time 5 to 7. τ 3 starts its execution and lock r x successfully at time 7. At time 8, a new instance of τ 1 is arrived and it is blocked by τ 3 because P L 1 is not higher than CL s = 3. The high speed H 1 of τ 1 = 0.9 is calculated by Equation ( 2) where B 3 = 2.5. Hence, from time 8 to the deadline of τ 1 , the processor speed is 0.9. At time 11.89, the processor speed is switched to the low speed L = 0.5 because the processor becomes idle. The schedule from time 12 to 19 is the same as that from time 0 to 7. Note that there is another high speed interval (16,19]. Finally, from time 20 to 22, another instance of τ 1 is executed at the low speed.

div.head: IV. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: The experiments described in this section are meant to assess the capabilities of BATS in scheduling of real-time tasks with shared resources on a DVS platform. The performance of our proposed BATS is compared with uniform slowdown with frequency inheritance (USFI) [9], multi-speed (MS) [4] and independent task set transformation (ITST). Where USFI and MS were designed for tasks with preemptible critical sections and non-preemptible critical sections, respectively. MS is the most closely related work of our research. We implemented USFI and MS by using EDF and SRP as the scheduling policy and the concurrency control protocol. ITST is a baseline approach. We transform the given set of dependent tasks (due to concurrent accesses to shared resources) into a corresponding set of independent tasks, and use EDF to schedule the transformed task set. Each task τ i is transformed into τ i by setting the worst-case computation amount of τ i as C i + B i . The execution speed of tasks is calculated by
div.formula: min sx∈S {s x : n i=1 Ci+Bi Ti
div.p: ≤ s x }. The performance of the above approaches are normalized with respect to the ITST for ease of comparison.

div.head: A. Simulation Setup
div.p: We have implemented a simulation of a DVS environment to evaluate the performance of our proposed BATS. In our simulation, a practical setting was chosen from the Marvell XScale PXA270 application processor [16]. Table I shows the available speeds and their power consumptions for Marvell XScale PXA270 processor. Note that the available processor speeds were normalized as s min =s 1 =0.17, s 2 =0.33, s 3 =0.5, s 4 =0.67, s 5 =0.83 and s 6 =s max =1. Since the overhead in speed switching is proportional to the difference between the original speed and the new speed, we consider the maximum switching overhead as 1ms for all cases. The primary performance metric of interest is the energy consumption of tasks, referred to as EnergyConsum. Let s(t) be the processor speed in time t, the energy consumption EnergyConsum can be calculated by simT ime 0 P C(s(t)) dt, where the simT ime is the simulation time. Note that the power consumption of a processor speed s j , i.e., P C(s j ), can be found in Table I. Similar to the work in [2], [9], we used a mixed workload with task periods belong to one of the three ranges: short (20 ∼ 100)ms, medium (100 ∼ 1000)ms, and long(1000 ∼ 5000)ms. The worst-case computation amounts of the tasks in the three categories were (1 ∼ 20)ms, (1 ∼ 100)ms, and (1 ∼ 1000)ms. For each task category, a task's period and worst-case computation amount were randomly selected from the corresponding ranges. Three types of task sets were generated: Type I consists of 10-20 tasks, Type II consists of 30-50 tasks, and Type III consists of 80-100 tasks. The generated tasks are uniformly distributed in the three categories. The utilization of each task set covered from light to heavy, i.e., from 20% to 80% with an increment of 10% 2 . We set the number of shared resources in the system is 5 to 10 to provide sufficient competition among tasks. The number of resources accessed by a task is selected randomly from 1 to 5. The position and the length of the critical sections within each task's execution were selected randomly. Note that the maximum length of any critical section z i,j was no larger than bf * C i , where bf is the blocking factor which specified the maximum percentage of the blocking interval could occupy in a task's execution time. In our simulation, the value of bf is set to 0.1 and 0.3. The simulation time is 1,000,000ms (exclude the speed calculation overheads). We generated 100 distinct task sets for each set of parameters, and their results were averaged. In Figures 3, 4 and5, the energy consumption of ITST is the worst because its heavier workload (each task was transformed by adding the worst case blocking time to its computation time.) and it will result in a higher execution speed. For ease of comparison, the experimental results are normalized with respect to the ITST. As we can observed, our proposed BATS outperforms all other approaches in all cases. The rank is BATS, MS, UFSI, and ITST (from the best to the worst).

div.head: B. Simulation Results
div.p: Both BATS and MS are scheduled tasks with two speeds, i.e., low speed and high speed. In general, the low speed is calculated by assuming that tasks are independent, and the high speed is calculated by considering tasks' executions with their worst-case blocking scenarios. Since the power consumption of tasks executed at the high speed is much higher than that of the low speed, i.e., P C(high speed) > P C(low speed). The more energy saving could be achieved if tasks are executed at the low speed more frequently. The UFSI performed worst in the simulation because the execution speeds are computed with tasks' worst-case blocking time. In other words, the UFSI always uses the high speed for task executions. varied with the number of tasks. Type I task sets (as shown in Figure 3), which consists of a small set of tasks (10-20 tasks), outperforms the results of type II and III task sets (as shown in Figure 4 and Figure 5). Where the number of tasks of type II and III are 30-50 and 80-100 tasks, respectively. It is because the competition among resources will be more intensely and the number of blockings will be increased when the number of tasks is increased. In particular, tasks will be executed at the high speeds more frequently under BATS and MS. However, our proposed BATS still save more energy than other approaches.

div.head: V. CONCLUSION
div.p: With the DVS technology, many processors can execute tasks at different speeds by adjusting its supply voltage. The execution of a real-time task can be completed late as long as its deadline is met. It provides an opportunity to reduce energy consumption by slowdown the processor speed without compromising performance. Hence, dynamic voltage scaling has become an attractive feature for many real-time system designs. In the recent decade, many excellent real-time scheduling algorithms have been proposed to support dynamic voltage scaling under different assumptions on DVS processor and/or on task models. However, relatively little work is done for scheduling and synchronizing of real-time tasks which are adopt widely in many application domains.

In this paper, a two-speed-based approach, called blockingaware two-speed (BATS), is proposed. BATS calculates a static low speed for task executions when there is no blocking occurs, and calculates a dynamic high speed whenever a blocking occurs. Under BATS, the processor operates at a high speed from the beginning of a blocking to the deadline of the blocked task or the time that the processor becomes idle. Compare with existing work, the high speed calculated by BATS is lower than other approaches and BATS also spent less time for executing tasks at high speeds. A series of experiments were performed to evaluate the capability of BATS. Based on the experimental results, the energy consumption under BATS is less than other existing work.
